title: Architecture standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's core architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding style, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also summarizes the canonical decision records (ADRs) relevant to cross-cutting platform behavior. The goal is a single, opinionated reference teams can use when designing services, onboarding models, or evaluating trade-offs for production deployments.

Scope

Applies to: all backend services, model-serving components, control plane services, and infra IaC that will run in production across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Out of scope: experimental prototypes, research notebooks (store in Google Drive) and one-off PoCs.

Principles

- Developer-first: standards should enable fast iteration while preventing common production mistakes.
- Predictability: reduce variability in latency, cost, and reliability across the platform.
- Observable: every service and model must expose telemetry required for SLOs and incident response.
- Safe defaults: default configs should be conservative and secure; opt-in for relaxations.

Standards (by area)

1) API Standards

- Design: public APIs follow RESTful resource model for control plane services and gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs. User-facing inference API remains HTTP/JSON REST for compatibility with SDKs.
- Versioning: use semantic-style version pathing for breaking changes (/v1/, /v2/). Deprecation windows: minimum 90 days for public endpoints.
- Error model: responses must use structured error body with fields: code (string), message (string), details (array). Map HTTP codes to categories (4xx client, 5xx server).
- Rate limits & quotas: endpoints must return X-RateLimit-* headers and follow standard 429 semantics. Default rate limit policy documented in product docs.
- Idempotency: all non-safe write operations should accept an Idempotency-Key header.
- Schema & validation: OpenAPI v3 for control plane endpoints; generate server/client stubs where feasible.

API Checklist (pre-release)

1. OpenAPI spec published and validated.
2. Auth and permission model documented.
3. Error codes enumerated.
4. Observability hooks instrumented (tracing, metrics).

2) Coding Standards

- Languages and formatting: use language-specific linters and formatters (gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, Black/flake8 for Python, prettier/eslint for TypeScript).
- Dependency management: pinned dependency files (go.mod, poetry.lock, package-lock.json) committed. No unchecked direct GitHub URL dependencies.
- Testing: unit tests >= 80% coverage for critical modules; integration tests for cross-service contracts. Tests must run in CI on pull requests.
- Packaging: build artifacts must be reproducible; binaries or Docker images versioned with semantic tags.
- Security: run SCA in CI; secrets must never be checked into repo. Use vault/KMS integrations for runtime secrets.

3) Infrastructure Standards

- IaC: Terraform for cloud infra (modules under eng-infra/terraform-and-iac). Modules must be reviewed and owned.
- Networking: services must support VPC isolation and use private subnets for internal components. Public endpoints require documented ingress rules.
- Capacity & autoscaling: set sensible default autoscaling with CPU/GPU/queue-based policies, and minimum/maximum bounds.
- GitOps: control-plane changes must be made via pull requests and automated apply pipelines.

4) Model-serving Standards

- Model packaging: every model must include a model-manifest.json with fields: model_name, version, architecture, expected_max_seq_len, quantization_profile, test_prompts (list).
- Container image: serve runtime images must include pinned runtime version, entrypoint that supports health and readiness probes, and an endpoint for /vitals/metrics.
- Latency tiers: categorize models into latency tiers (latency-sensitive < 100ms per token, batch-friendly 100ms–500ms, throughput-optimized > 500ms per token). Route according to workload policies.
- KV/prefix caching: models with heavy prefix reuse must implement prefix cache bindings (see: caching design ADR).
- Rollouts: use canary-by-traffic with progressive steps (5%, 25%, 100%) and automated quality checks (synthetic prompts, end-to-end smoke).

Model Onboarding Checklist

1. Model manifest and test prompts provided.
2. Benchmark results (p50/p95 token latency, throughput at batch sizes) attached.
3. Quantization profile recommendations included.
4. Cost estimate per-100k tokens documented.

5) Observability Standards

- Tracing: all service requests must propagate distributed traces (OpenTelemetry). Tag traces with request_id, customer_id (when present), model_version, and route.
- Metrics: expose prometheus metrics with standardized labels (service, route, model, env). Key metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms_{p50,p95,p99}, token_count, model_cache_hit_rate, batch_size_distribution.
- Logs: structured JSON logs (timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, msg, attrs). Avoid logging PII.
- Dashboards & Alerts: each service must publish a per-route dashboard and alerts tied to SLO burn (see SLOs below).

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

- Service SLOs: default production SLOs for inference paths: availability 99.95% (monthly), p95 request latency targets per latency tier (latency-sensitive: p95 < 200ms; batch-friendly: p95 < 700ms).
- Error budget policy: errors include 5xx responses and timeout throttles. On >50% error budget consumption in a 7-day window, trigger reliability runbook and rollback any recent rollouts.
- Throughput & cost: measure cost-per-1M tokens and publish monthly. Use quantization and batching to meet target cost reductions before increasing capacity.

Decision Records (ADRs) Summary

- ADR 001: Default Inference Protocol (2025-06-10) — chose HTTP/JSON REST for public inference to preserve SDK simplicity; internal gRPC for high-throughput components.
- ADR 012: Kernel Selection Strategy (2026-01-15) — adopt runtime kernel probe and fallback to generic kernels when specialized kernels fail.
- ADR 018: Model Quantization Policy (2026-03-04) — adopt quantization profiles per model family; default safe profile Q4_0 for production.
- ADR 024: Routing & Fallback Policy (2026-06-20) — smart routing by latency tier, cost tier, and region with automated fallback chains.

Each ADR contains motivation, alternatives considered, consequences, and owner. Refer to the ADR folder for full text and links.

Operational Playbooks and Runbooks

- Incident: standard incident process includes immediate mitigation (traffic diversion to fallback model or region), paging oncall, post-incident triage, and ADR if systemic change is required.
- Rollback: documented rollback steps for model and service releases. Always include data retention considerations when rolling back model outputs.

Templates and Examples

- Model manifest example (inline):
  {
    "model_name": "gptx-8b",
    "version": "2026-03-01",
    "architecture": "transformer",
    "expected_max_seq_len": "8192",
    "quantization_profile": "Q4_0",
    "test_prompts": ["summarize: ...", "classify: ..."]
  }

- OpenAPI snippet: endpoints must include summary, operationId, and x-owner tags for automated routing in the API gateway.

Ownership and Review Cycle

- Document owner: Architecture Guild (contact: aisha.patel@redwood.ai).
- Review cadence: quarterly review for standards; ADRs reviewed ad-hoc when major architectural trade-offs occur.
